blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A classification prompt gets most tickets right but keeps mislabelling sarcastic ones. Which first step fits best?

options.text: Swap in a larger model and see whether the sarcastic cases improve
options.says: Ruled out because a larger model is the fix only for "Correct instructions, correct context, still a capability or speed miss", which nobody has established.

options.text: Leave the wording alone and sort the failures against the diagnosis table
options.says: Diagnosis comes before any change: the failures are read against the four causes (page 4), without altering the prompt.

options.text: Add twenty more examples of sarcasm and rewrite the instructions at the same time
options.says: Ruled out because the method is to "Change one thing at a time", and this changes two at once.

options.text: Rewrite the instructions to name sarcasm outright and see whether the labels settle
options.says: Ruled out because the page puts "Diagnose first: four causes" ahead of any edit, and an instruction rewrite is a guess until the cause is known.

questions.stem: A team asks for a label and gets free text, and their parser breaks when a reply starts with "Sure!". They call Claude Opus 5.5. Which pair of actions best fits the module?

options.text: Request longer replies and trim them by length
options.says: Ruled out because the fix for a stray preamble is to "ask for the answer inside tags, and strip what slips through in code", not to trim by length.

options.text: Prefill the reply with an opening brace so it cannot start with chat
options.says: Ruled out because prefilled responses on the last assistant turn "are no longer supported" from Claude 4.6 and return a 400 error.

options.text: State the exact shape up front, then check and clean the output in code
options.says: Specify the format in the prompt and check it in code, and page 2 adds stripping a stray preamble.

options.text: Remove the parser and rely on the model to answer with the label only
options.says: Ruled out because "Code that consumes the output must still validate it".

origin.section: Say what the output looks like

questions.stem: A prompt for brainstorming product names returns ten near-identical suggestions. A colleague points out that the team's research prompt, which says to be precise and cite sources, works well. Which change fits?

options.text: Lower the randomness setting so every name is the most probable one
options.says: Ruled out because "the approach that suits extraction (precision, low variety) works against ideation", and the most probable name is the least varied; module 1 adds that the models this course uses do not accept sampling settings.

options.text: Copy the research wording, "be precise and cite sources", into this prompt
options.says: Ruled out because an instruction that helps a research prompt "can be noise in a brainstorm" (page 3, third trap).

options.text: Supply three near-identical sample names so the model sees the target
options.says: Ruled out because examples must "vary enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns", and near-identical samples teach one pattern (page 2).

options.text: Ask for many varied options first, then evaluate them in a second pass
options.says: Brainstorming wants breadth first and judgment later, with a second pass to evaluate (page 3, strategy per task type).

questions.stem: A drafting prompt produces bland correspondence. The team wants replies in a specific house style. Which addition is most likely to get it?

options.text: A stronger role line: "You are the best business writer alive"
options.says: Ruled out because "A role is a request, not a credential", and it names no target to copy.

options.text: Three to five real past emails, wrapped in example tags
options.says: A handful of real past emails in tags puts the target house voice into the context, which the page says is how examples steer tone and structure (page 2).

options.text: A longer list of style adjectives: warm, crisp, confident, human
options.says: Ruled out because "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" is the first trap of page 1.

options.text: A higher effort setting so Claude thinks harder about tone
options.says: Ruled out because thinking is "where Claude decides when and how much to think, steered by the effort parameter", which sets reasoning depth and not voice.

origin.section: Give Claude a role, for what it is

questions.stem: A prompt asks Claude how many units of a product the warehouse holds right now, and it answers with a confident, wrong number. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Wire in a query against the live database and let the model phrase the result
options.says: The count lives in a system the model cannot see, so the job needs a feature the prompt cannot give: a lookup, with the model only phrasing the result (the diagnosis table's wrong-feature row).

options.text: Ask for a confidence score on each count so that doubtful ones can be dropped later
options.says: Ruled out because for a missing feature "A cleverer prompt does not fix it", and a score from the same model adds no data.

options.text: Move to the largest tier, whose knowledge is the most complete
options.says: Ruled out because the wrong-model cause is "Correct instructions, correct context, still a capability or speed miss", and no tier knows a private count.

options.text: Tell Claude to answer only with the numbers it is certain about
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "Fix the feature, not the phrasing".
